title: Workshop Overview
content:
The problem Small forums and classified-ad sites receive thousands of images every month. Manual moderation is slow, needs people, and easily misses violent or offensive images. ImageGuard automates it: every image is moderated in about 1–2 seconds after upload.
What you will build A static website served through CloudFront, sign-in with Cognito (OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE). Users upload images directly to S3 with a presigned URL; images never pass through API Gateway or Lambda. An S3 Event triggers the process-image Lambda: it calls DetectModerationLabels, and only if the image is allowed calls DetectLabels, then stores the result in DynamoDB. Violating images get the REJECTED status and trigger an SNS email. Failures after 2 retries go to an SQS DLQ. CloudWatch provides logs, 5 custom metrics (EMF), 7 alarms and 1 dashboard. What you will learn Topic Content Event-driven architecture S3 Event → asynchronous Lambda, retries and Dead-Letter Queue Security Least privilege per Lambda, presigned URLs, JWT Authorizer, OAC, confused-deputy protection AI without training a model Amazon Rekognition Content Moderation and Label Detection Operations Embedded Metric Format, CloudWatch Alarm → SNS, dashboard Cost AWS Pricing Calculator, lifecycle rules, log retention, HTTP API Contents Prerequisites Architecture Step-by-step lab Testing and troubleshooting Cost Clean-up Demo video

Building a Collaborative Multi-Agent System with Amazon Bedrock and AWS Step Functions Author: Nguyễn Ngọc Tân – https://builder.aws.com/community/@kevintan1511 Posted on: Facebook – 18/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/share/p/14vDq2GGn9q/?mibextid=wwXIfr Figure: Architecture of the collaborative multi-agent system, with an orchestrator coordinating specialized agents.
Introduction As generative AI matures, applications are moving from a single prompt to multi-agent systems. Instead of one large model doing everything, several specialized agents work together, for example a Researcher Agent, an Analyst Agent and a Writer Agent. This post shows how to orchestrate Amazon Bedrock Agents with AWS Step Functions to build a scalable multi-agent workflow that solves complex, multi-step business problems.
Why Orchestrate Multiple Agents? Separation of concerns: each agent has its own prompt and its own knowledge base. Cost efficiency: send simple tasks to smaller, faster models (such as Claude 3 Haiku) and complex reasoning to larger ones (such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Resilience: AWS Step Functions adds built-in error handling, retries and state management around every agent call. High-Level Architecture Trigger: Amazon API Gateway receives a complex user request and triggers an AWS Lambda function. Orchestrator: the Lambda function starts an AWS Step Functions state machine. Agent 1 (Data Retrieval): a Bedrock Agent queries an enterprise Knowledge Base (RAG) to collect context. Agent 2 (Processing): a second Bedrock Agent analyzes the retrieved data with specific business logic. Output: the final synthesized answer is stored in Amazon DynamoDB and returned to the user. Implementation Cheatsheet: Invoking an Agent with Boto3 To call Amazon Bedrock Agents from a Step Functions workflow, you typically use AWS Lambda tasks. This Python snippet invokes one Bedrock Agent and collects its streamed answer:
import boto3 import uuid def invoke_bedrock_agent(agent_id, agent_alias_id, session_id, prompt): client = boto3.client('bedrock-agent-runtime') response = client.invoke_agent( agentId=agent_id, agentAliasId=agent_alias_id, sessionId=session_id, inputText=prompt ) completion = "" for event in response.get('completion'): if 'chunk' in event: chunk = event['chunk'] completion += chunk['bytes'].decode() return completion # Example usage session_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) result = invoke_bedrock_agent( agent_id='ABC123XYZ', agent_alias_id='TSTALIASID', session_id=session_id, prompt='Analyze the following financial dataset for anomalies...' ) print(result) Notes from the Article The agent ID and alias ID in the snippet are placeholders; replace them with your own agent and alias. Model names such as Claude 3 Haiku and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are examples; check which models are available in your Region and account. In the workflow, each agent runs as a Lambda task, and Step Functions passes one agent’s output to the next state, with retries and error handling around every call. Each agent needs an IAM role with the right permissions, and Agent 1 needs a Knowledge Base set up before it can retrieve data. My Takeaway Splitting a complex problem across specialized agents is easier to manage than one giant prompt, and Step Functions provides the reliable control layer (state, retries, error handling) that keeps the whole workflow dependable. Source: Building a Collaborative Multi-Agent System with Amazon Bedrock and AWS Step Functions – AWS Builder Center (08/11/2026) https://builder.aws.com/content/3LmigErfNLw8Y7oyb2B3jTPHZUH/building-a-collaborative-multi-agent-system-with-amazon-bedrock-and-aws-step-functions

content:
Building a Scalable RAG Pipeline with Amazon Bedrock and LangChain on AWS Author: Nguyễn Ngọc Tân – https://builder.aws.com/community/@kevintan1511 Posted on: AWS Study Group VN (Facebook) – 21/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19c9vku5gi/ Figure: The RAG pipeline in five phases: setup, ingestion, embedding and retrieval, orchestration and generation, and deployment and scaling.
Introduction Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) connects Large Language Models (LLMs) with private knowledge bases, so a model can answer from your own documents instead of only from what it learned in training. This post explores how to build a robust, scalable RAG workflow on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and LangChain.
Architecture Overview The system uses a serverless architecture designed for high availability and low latency:
Data ingestion and processing: documents are stored in Amazon S3 and processed with distributed compute. Embedding and retrieval: Amazon Bedrock foundation models, such as Amazon Titan Embeddings, turn text into vectors and build a semantic index. Orchestration: LangChain manages the prompt, the retrieved context and the call to the LLM. Implementation Steps Set up Amazon Bedrock access: enable the foundation models you need in the AWS Management Console. Configure LangChain: connect your Python environment to the Bedrock APIs with Boto3. Deploy the pipeline: package the solution as serverless functions for real-time querying. Example: A Minimal RAG Chain This short example is for illustration. Install the libraries first with pip install boto3 langchain-aws langchain-community faiss-cpu, then replace the model ID with a model you have enabled in Bedrock.
import json import boto3 from langchain_aws import BedrockEmbeddings, ChatBedrock from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1") # Embedding model (vectorizes text) and LLM (writes the answer) embeddings = BedrockEmbeddings(client=bedrock, model_id="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0") llm = ChatBedrock(client=bedrock, model_id="<your-bedrock-model-id>") # Index a few document chunks (in a real pipeline, load them from S3) chunks = [ "Refunds are processed within 5 business days.", "Customer support is available on weekdays from 8:00 to 17:00.", ] retriever = FAISS.from_texts(chunks, embeddings).as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 2}) prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template( "Answer using only the context below.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}" ) chain = prompt | llm | StrOutputParser() def answer(question): docs = retriever.invoke(question) context = "\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs) return chain.invoke({"context": context, "question": question}) # Step 3: expose answer() through AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway def lambda_handler(event, context): question = json.loads(event["body"])["question"] return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"answer": answer(question)})} Conclusion By combining AWS managed AI services with orchestration frameworks such as LangChain, developers can quickly deploy secure, enterprise-grade generative AI applications with very little infrastructure to manage.
Notes from the Article The article describes the design at a high level. A production system also needs document chunking, access control and monitoring. In the example, FAISS keeps the index in memory for demonstration only; a real deployment would use a managed vector store. Model IDs and library versions change over time, so check the current Bedrock and LangChain documentation before reusing the code. My Takeaway RAG lets an LLM answer from private documents without retraining it, and Bedrock with LangChain keeps the pipeline small enough to run serverlessly. Source: Building a Scalable RAG Pipeline with Amazon Bedrock and LangChain on AWS – AWS Builder Center (22/10/2026) https://builder.aws.com/content/3L2CYIssIZJ1v5zQhZ4dYa7MiJx/building-a-scalable-rag-pipeline-with-amazon-bedrock-and-langchain-on-aws

title: Proposal
content:
ImageGuard – AI-Powered Image Moderation and Labeling on AWS Serverless Status: Proposal v2.0.
1. Overview ImageGuard is a serverless web application for sites where people post pictures, such as classified-ad boards, forums and student clubs. It checks every uploaded image automatically and tags it with searchable labels. As soon as a photo arrives, Amazon Rekognition, a ready-made computer-vision service, runs two checks:
Moderation: looks for unsafe content such as violence, explicit material, weapons or drugs. A flagged image is stored as REJECTED and the administrator receives an email. Labeling: for images that pass, it produces descriptive labels (for example Laptop, Bicycle, Book), so owners can find their pictures by keyword. Outcomes are saved in Amazon DynamoDB and appear in the web interface within a few seconds. The design is event-driven and serverless: there is nothing to patch or keep running, and the bill follows real usage. 2. Problem Statement Sites with user uploads collect a steady flow of pictures. Checking them by hand is slow and costly, and moderators end up looking at harmful material. Without a filter, unsafe pictures can go public and damage both users and the platform’s name. Most uploads carry no caption or tags, so older pictures are almost impossible to find again. Our answer: let AI do both jobs the moment a picture is uploaded. Unsafe images are stopped before anyone sees them, and safe images are labeled so they can be searched. 2.1. Who Uses ImageGuard Role What they do What they get Uploader Signs in, uploads pictures, searches their own images Instant feedback and automatic labels Administrator Receives email alerts Only flagged images need attention Development team Builds and operates the system A low-cost design with no servers to maintain 3. Objectives & Scope 3.1. Objectives Deliver an automatic flow, Upload → AI moderation → AI labeling → Storage → Display/Search, built wholly on AWS. Follow the AWS Well-Architected Framework, with extra care for the Security pillar (least-privilege IAM, nothing public, no credentials in code). Give the team full visibility through Amazon CloudWatch (logs, metrics, alarms) and Amazon SNS email alerts. Hold the running cost near USD 6–7 per month for the expected workload (Section 6). Produce a bilingual, step-by-step guide so anyone can rebuild the system. 3.2. Success Criteria Criterion Target Time from upload to visible result ≤ 10 seconds Violating images blocked on the test set ≥ 90% Valid images blocked by mistake (false positives) on the test set ≤ 10% Images processed without manual help (none stuck in PENDING or FAILED) ≥ 95% API call without a valid sign-in Rejected (HTTP 401) One user reading another user’s images or results Impossible Violating image found Email alert reaches the administrator Direct Internet access to the S3 buckets Blocked (Block Public Access) Monthly cost for the expected workload ≤ USD 10 3.3. Scope In scope Out of scope JPG and PNG images up to 5 MB Video and animated GIFs Content moderation and automatic labeling Face recognition (biometric and privacy-sensitive) Searching by label inside a user’s own images Searching across all users’ images Sign-up and sign-in with Amazon Cognito A dedicated admin console and appeals against decisions One Region: us-east-1 Multi-Region deployment and disaster recovery 3.4. Assumptions and Constraints The system runs in a single AWS account covered by credits, in Region us-east-1. Testing uses a small set of the team’s own or freely licensed images, mixing normal and borderline cases. The target is a small community, about 3,000 images per month, not internet scale. Moderation uses a 60% confidence threshold and labeling uses 80%; both can be tuned. 4. Solution Architecture Figure 1: ImageGuard architecture diagram, drawn with AWS Architecture Icons.
4.1. AWS Services and Rationale Service Role in the system Why it was chosen Amazon S3 Holds uploaded images in a private bucket and also hosts the static website Extremely durable and cheap; its S3 Events start the processing Amazon CloudFront Delivers the site over HTTPS and reaches S3 through Origin Access Control (OAC) Keeps the website bucket private; HTTPS at no extra charge; inside the Always Free allowance (1 TB/month) Amazon Cognito (User Pool) Handles sign-up and sign-in and issues JWT tokens Managed identity, free up to 10,000 MAU, and the app never touches passwords Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Exposes the endpoints the web app calls, guarded by a Cognito JWT authorizer About USD 1 per million requests, much cheaper than REST APIs, with built-in Cognito support AWS Lambda (Python 3.12) Runs three functions: presign-upload, process-image and get-images No servers, billed per call, scales on its own Amazon Rekognition DetectModerationLabels for safety checks and DetectLabels for tagging Ready-made AI with no training; reads pictures straight from S3; available on the Free plan Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) Keeps each user’s moderation results and labels Serverless NoSQL, pay per request, fast, 25 GB free Amazon SQS Acts as the Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) for events that keep failing Nothing is lost, and failed events can be replayed Amazon CloudWatch Collects logs and metrics, runs alarms, shows the dashboard One place to watch everything, as the workshop requires Amazon SNS Emails the administrator about rejected images and fired alarms Simple setup; 1,000 emails per month free AWS IAM Gives every Lambda its own least-privilege role The security base of the whole design Why us-east-1: it is usually the cheapest Region and offers every service we need. The extra ~200 ms of latency from Vietnam hardly matters, because the website is served from CloudFront edge locations (including Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City) and AI analysis is the slowest step anyway. For real users in Vietnam the team would move to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) for lower latency and personal-data rules; Region and resource names are environment variables, so the code stays the same. 4.2. Data Flow The step numbers below match the arrows in Figure 1.
HTTPS (static web): the user opens the site through CloudFront, which reads the private imageguard-web bucket via OAC. Sign in → JWT: the user signs in with the Cognito User Pool and receives a JWT token. POST /upload-url: the web app calls API Gateway with the token, and the JWT authorizer checks it. 3a. Invoke: API Gateway calls the presign-upload Lambda. 3b. PutItem (PENDING): the Lambda writes a PENDING record to DynamoDB and returns a presigned URL, valid for 5 minutes, for the key uploads/{userId}/{imageId}.jpg. PUT image: the browser uploads the file straight to S3 (imageguard-images) using that URL, so it never passes through Lambda or API Gateway. S3 Event (ObjectCreated): a new object under the uploads/ prefix triggers the process-image Lambda asynchronously. DetectModerationLabels + DetectLabels: process-image asks Rekognition to moderate the image and, if it is clean, to label it. 6a. Read image: Rekognition reads the picture directly from S3. A moderation label in a blocked category with confidence ≥ 60% means REJECTED; otherwise up to 10 labels with confidence ≥ 80% are kept. UpdateItem (APPROVED / REJECTED): the result, reason and labels are written to DynamoDB. Publish alert if REJECTED: an email goes to the administrator through the SNS topic imageguard-alerts. On failure (after 2 retries): the event is sent to the SQS DLQ so it can be replayed. GET /images (JWT): the web app asks for the user’s images. 10a. Invoke: API Gateway calls the get-images Lambda. 10b. Query by userId: the Lambda queries DynamoDB with the userId taken from the token, filters by label, and returns short-lived presigned GET URLs. Logs & Metrics (all Lambdas): every function reports to CloudWatch. Alarm: a CloudWatch alarm notifies the administrator through SNS. Throughout, each Lambda runs under its own IAM execution role with least privilege (red dashed line in the diagram). 4.3. Security Design (Security Pillar) Principle How ImageGuard applies it Least privilege Each Lambda has its own role. process-image is limited to s3:GetObject on uploads/*, the two Rekognition actions rekognition:DetectModerationLabels and rekognition:DetectLabels, dynamodb:UpdateItem on one table and sns:Publish on one topic. presign-upload may only use s3:PutObject on uploads/* and dynamodb:PutItem. get-images may only use dynamodb:Query and s3:GetObject Rekognition limitation Rekognition’s image APIs cannot be restricted to a resource, so "Resource": "*" is unavoidable. To compensate, only the two needed actions are allowed, never rekognition:* Nothing public Both buckets use Block Public Access. Only CloudFront can read the website bucket (OAC). The image bucket is reachable only through short-lived presigned URLs Sign-in and data isolation Every API call needs a Cognito JWT. userId always comes from the token’s sub claim and never from the request, so users cannot see each other’s data No hard-coded credentials Lambdas use IAM roles with temporary credentials. Bucket, table and topic names are environment variables. The GitHub repository holds no access keys and includes a .gitignore Encryption S3 and DynamoDB encrypt data at rest by default, and all traffic uses HTTPS/TLS Input checks Presigned URLs fix the image Content-Type, and the Lambda verifies size (≤ 5 MB) and format before calling the AI Privacy No face recognition and no biometric data are stored Why are the Lambdas outside a VPC? Nothing in this design needs a private network: the functions reach S3, DynamoDB, Rekognition and SNS over HTTPS, with access controlled by IAM. A VPC would add NAT Gateway or interface endpoint fees (tens of USD a month) with little security benefit here. The team keeps it as a future option if compliance requires it.
4.4. Mapping to the AWS Well-Architected Framework Pillar How it is applied Operational Excellence Logs kept 14 days, a dashboard, alarms and a guide that can be repeated Security See Section 4.3 Reliability Event-driven flow, two automatic Lambda retries, a DLQ for failed events and explicit PENDING/APPROVED/REJECTED/FAILED states Performance Efficiency Uploads go directly to S3, Rekognition reads from S3 (the Lambda never downloads images), and DynamoDB is queried by key Cost Optimization Fully serverless; DetectLabels runs only for images that pass moderation; S3 Lifecycle, 14-day logs and AWS Budgets Sustainability No idle resources; compute runs only when an image arrives 4.5. Why Amazon Rekognition The first plan used Amazon Bedrock to process invoices. While testing, the team found its account had a Bedrock quota of 0, and the request to raise it was declined. The team moved to Amazon Rekognition, a ready-made AI service that works on the current account and was verified in the console, and reused most of the serverless design. The episode is written up in the Troubleshooting part of the workshop.
4.6. Monitoring and Alerting Plan Signal Threshold Action process-image Lambda errors ≥ 1 in 5 minutes CloudWatch alarm, email through SNS Messages visible in the SQS DLQ ≥ 1 Email through SNS, replay the failed event API Gateway 5XX responses ≥ 5 in 5 minutes Email through SNS, check the Lambda logs process-image duration (p95) > 8 seconds Investigate, because the end-to-end target is 10 seconds Custom metric: rejected images Any increase Review on the CloudWatch dashboard AWS Budgets 80% of USD 10 Email, pause testing and review usage 4.7. Moderation Policy The proposed default policy uses Rekognition’s top-level moderation categories. The list lives in an environment variable, so the team can change it without editing code.
Category Default action Explicit REJECTED and email the administrator Violence, Visually Disturbing, Hate Symbols REJECTED and email the administrator Drugs & Tobacco REJECTED and email the administrator Alcohol, Gambling, Rude Gestures Allowed, but the label is stored for review 5. Plan & Timeline Internship period: 14/09/2026 – 04/12/2026. The workshop is due on 19/11/2026, which leaves 15 days before the internship certificate is needed.
5.1. Roles Member Main responsibility Member A Team lead, integration, IAM and security Member B process-image Lambda, Rekognition integration, test images and accuracy evaluation Member C Cognito, API Gateway and the presign-upload and get-images Lambdas Member D Static web UI, S3 and CloudFront (OAC) Member E CloudWatch, SNS, DLQ, cost estimate and clean-up guide Every member should be able to explain the whole architecture, not just their own part. 5.2. Weekly Timeline Internship week Dates Tasks Output Week 7 26/10 – 01/11 Settle the topic and write proposal v1.0; try Bedrock and find the zero quota Proposal v1.0, incident notes Week 8 02/11 – 08/11 Ask for a quota increase (declined); switch to Rekognition and write proposal v2.0; create S3, DynamoDB and IAM roles; build process-image with its S3 trigger Proposal v2.0, working image pipeline Week 9 09/11 – 15/11 Cognito, API Gateway and the two API Lambdas; static site and CloudFront; CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboard; SNS and DLQ; testing; AWS Pricing Calculator; demo video End-to-end demo, video, cost table Week 10 16/11 – 19/11 Write the bilingual workshop guide (steps, testing, clean-up), take screenshots, finish the diagram, peer review Workshop submitted on 19/11 Week 10–12 20/11 – 04/12 Apply mentor feedback, finish blogs and worklogs, clean up resources Final report 6. Cost Estimation Workload scenario: a small forum or classified-ad site with about 3,000 images per month (~100 a day, 1 MB each, about 3% violating) and roughly 30,000 views and searches. Region us-east-1, on-demand prices, before Free Tier and credits.
Service Assumptions Estimated cost (USD/month) Amazon Rekognition 3,000 DetectModerationLabels + ~2,910 DetectLabels calls × USD 0.001 per image 5.91 AWS Lambda 36,000 invocations, ~3,200 GB-seconds 0.06 (within the free tier) Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) 33,000 requests 0.03 Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) ~6,000 write and 30,000 read units, under 1 GB 0.01 Amazon S3 3 GB (30-day lifecycle), 3,000 PUT, 6,000 GET 0.09 Amazon CloudWatch 0.5 GB logs, 3 alarms, 3 custom metrics, 1 dashboard 0.27 (mostly within the free tier) Amazon CloudFront ~2 GB transfer, 40,000 requests 0.00 (Always Free) Amazon Cognito Under 10,000 MAU 0.00 Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS About 100 emails or messages 0.00 Total ≈ USD 6.40/month (≈ USD 76/year) During development and the demo (under 300 images), Rekognition costs about USD 0.60 and the account’s credits cover everything. AWS Pricing Calculator link: [to be added after the estimate is created] Cost Optimization Strategy Fully serverless: no EC2, NAT Gateway or other always-on resources. Moderate first, label second: rejected images skip DetectLabels, saving one AI call each. Rekognition reads images directly from S3, so each Lambda run is short (~2 seconds) and needs only 256 MB. An S3 Lifecycle rule deletes images after 30 days (or archives them to S3 Glacier if they must be kept). CloudWatch Logs are kept 14 days instead of the default “Never expire”. An HTTP API instead of a REST API (about 70% cheaper). An AWS Budgets alert at USD 10, and clean-up right after grading. Beyond 1 million images per month, Rekognition’s tiered pricing lowers the per-image price automatically. 7. Risks & Mitigation Risk Impact Mitigation Rekognition blocks good images or misses bad ones Frustrated users, or harmful content slips through Thresholds and blocked categories are environment variables that can be tuned; accuracy is measured on the test set Quotas on new accounts (already hit with Bedrock) AI calls fail Rekognition confirmed working on the account; retry with backoff when throttled S3 → Lambda → S3 loop Runaway cost The trigger covers only uploads/, and the Lambda never writes back to S3 Access keys pushed to GitHub Account takeover IAM roles only, a .gitignore, and a review before each commit Test images that infringe copyright or are too disturbing Legal and ethical problems Use the team’s own or freely licensed photos; test with mild categories (alcohol, tobacco, toy weapons) Unexpected charges Loss of credits AWS Budgets and a clean-up checklist Abuse of the upload endpoint (spam, oversized files) Cost spikes and noisy data Presigned URLs expire in 5 minutes and fix type and size; API Gateway throttling; per-user limits A user disputes a rejection Loss of trust Each REJECTED record keeps the reason and confidence; an admin review flow is listed as a future improvement Very little time (~2 weeks) Missed deadline Build the MVP first and extras later; every week has a clear deliverable Members still new to AWS Delays and unanswered mentor questions Learn while building, hold peer reviews, and have everyone explain the full design 8. Expected Outcomes A working web app: sign in, upload an image, and get either a block with an email alert or a labeled, searchable picture. Monitoring in place, with a CloudWatch dashboard, alarms and email alerts. A bilingual workshop guide that others can follow from scratch, covering testing, troubleshooting and clean-up. New skills for the team: event-driven serverless design, least-privilege IAM, AWS AI services, monitoring, cost control, and adapting when a service is quota-limited. 9. Future Improvements An admin review page and an appeal flow for rejected images. Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels for categories specific to the platform. AWS WAF in front of CloudFront to block abusive traffic. AWS X-Ray tracing to spot slow steps in the pipeline. Infrastructure as Code (AWS SAM or CloudFormation) so the whole stack deploys with one command. A move to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) for lower latency and local data requirements.

title: Architecture
content:
Figure: ImageGuard architecture diagram
The diagram has 5 groups: Frontend, Authentication & API, Compute, Storage & AI, Notification & Monitoring. CloudFront sits outside the Region box because it is a global service. Arrow colors show the flow type: blue for upload, green for viewing, orange for AI processing, dashed grey for monitoring, dashed red for IAM permissions. Arrows point in the request direction.
Request flow (matches the numbers on the diagram) # From → To Description 1 User → CloudFront → S3 imageguard-web The browser loads the static site (HTML/JS) over HTTPS. CloudFront reads the private web bucket via OAC 2 User → Cognito Sign-in with Cognito Managed Login (Authorization Code + PKCE), returning JWTs (ID token + access token) 3 User → API Gateway Calls POST /upload-url with the access token; the JWT Authorizer checks signature, issuer and audience 3a API Gateway → presign-upload The Lambda takes userId from the sub claim and generates imageId (UUID) 3b presign-upload → DynamoDB Writes a PENDING item, then returns a presigned PUT URL (5 minutes) for the key uploads/{sub}/{imageId}.jpg 4 User → S3 imageguard-images The browser PUTs the image straight to S3 with the presigned URL; the image never passes through API Gateway or Lambda 5 S3 → process-image S3 Event ObjectCreated:Put (prefix uploads/, suffix .jpg) invokes the Lambda asynchronously 6 process-image → Rekognition Calls DetectModerationLabels (60% threshold). If nothing is blocked, calls DetectLabels (up to 10 labels, ≥ 80%) 6a Rekognition → S3 Rekognition reads the image from S3 itself (S3Object); the Lambda never downloads it 7 process-image → DynamoDB Conditional UpdateItem on status = PENDING → APPROVED or REJECTED 8 process-image → SNS → Admin Sends the alert email only when the image is REJECTED and the DynamoDB update succeeded 9 process-image → SQS DLQ After 2 failed retries the event goes to the dead-letter queue, kept for 14 days 10 User → API Gateway Calls GET /images with the access token (shares the arrow with step 3) 10a API Gateway → get-images The Lambda takes userId from the sub claim 10b get-images → DynamoDB Query by userId, newest first, at most 50 items; only APPROVED images get a presigned GET URL (5 minutes) 10c User → S3 imageguard-images The browser downloads approved images with the presigned GET URL 11 Lambda → CloudWatch Structured JSON logs and 5 custom metrics via Embedded Metric Format (EMF) 12 CloudWatch → SNS 7 alarms email on ALARM and on return to OK – IAM → Lambda Each Lambda has its own least-privilege IAM role Why each service Service Role Why Alternatives considered Amazon S3 Stores images and the static site 99.999999999% durability, cheap, S3 Events trigger processing, Lifecycle deletes old images EBS/EFS: must be attached to a server, more expensive AWS Lambda Runs the 3 functions No servers to manage, scales with the number of images, pay per invocation; almost USD 0 when idle EC2/ECS: runs 24/7 even with no images Amazon Rekognition Moderation and labeling Ready-made content moderation models, no training data, pay per image Amazon Bedrock: quota 0 on new accounts (see 5.5); training our own model: needs data and GPUs Amazon DynamoDB Stores status and labels Serverless, on-demand pricing per request, fast queries by userId, conditional writes RDS: instance runs 24/7, needs a VPC Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) API for the web app Built-in JWT Authorizer for Cognito, CORS, throttling; about 70% cheaper than REST API REST API: more features than needed; Lambda Function URL: no JWT Authorizer Amazon Cognito Sign-up and sign-in Managed Login UI, OAuth 2.0 + PKCE, no passwords stored by us Custom login: high security risk Amazon CloudFront Serves the site HTTPS by default, edge caching near users, OAC keeps the web bucket private S3 static website hosting: HTTP only, bucket must be public Amazon SNS Alert email Emails the administrator with a few lines of code and also receives CloudWatch alarms Amazon SES: suited to per-user emails, requires verifying the sender identity Amazon SQS Dead-letter queue Keeps failed events 14 days for inspection and reprocessing, so no image is lost No DLQ: an async Lambda event is dropped after the retries run out Amazon CloudWatch Logs, metrics, alarms, dashboard Lambda logs here by default; EMF turns logs into metrics without API calls External tools: extra setup and permissions AWS IAM Permissions One role per Lambda, scoped to exactly the resources it needs One shared role: a compromised function would get the rights of all three Data model (DynamoDB imageguard-images) Attribute Type Meaning userId String – Partition key Cognito sub claim. One partition per user, so Query only returns that user’s images imageId String – Sort key UUID generated by presign-upload, also the S3 file name status String PENDING → APPROVED or REJECTED createdAt, processedAt String (ISO 8601) When the upload URL was requested and when moderation finished moderationLabels List Moderation labels from Rekognition (name, parent category, confidence) labels List Content labels (name, confidence), only for valid images blockedCategories List Top-level categories that caused the block, e.g. Violence reason String BLOCKED_CATEGORY, TOO_LARGE (> 5 MB) or INVALID_IMAGE:<error> (not an image) No Global Secondary Index is needed: every query in the system is by userId, which is exactly the partition key.
Moderation policy Blocked top-level categories: Explicit, Violence, Visually Disturbing, Drugs & Tobacco, Hate Symbols (environment variable BLOCKED_CATEGORIES, changeable without code changes). Alcohol is allowed but its labels are still stored for administrators. Moderate first, label second: violating images do not cost an extra DetectLabels call. Security design Principle Implementation Least privilege One IAM role per Lambda, no AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole Private data Both buckets use Block all public access, ACLs disabled, SSE-S3, a bucket policy enforcing HTTPS Authentication The JWT Authorizer validates the issuer (User Pool) and audience (App client); userId always comes from the sub claim, never from the body Safe upload The server signs the presigned URL; it can PUT only one server-chosen key, expires after 5 minutes and requires image/jpeg Confused deputy The Lambda resource-based policy uses aws:SourceArn + aws:SourceAccount Recursive trigger The trigger only covers prefix uploads/, and process-image cannot write to S3 Idempotency UpdateItem conditioned on status = PENDING: duplicate events or overwrites cannot change a result Web CloudFront OAC, HTTPS, SecurityHeadersPolicy (HSTS, X-Frame-Options…), the frontend only uses textContent to avoid XSS Permissions per Lambda Lambda Allowed Not allowed process-image s3:GetObject (uploads/*), 2 Rekognition actions, dynamodb:UpdateItem, sns:Publish, sqs:SendMessage, its own logs PutObject, Query, PutItem presign-upload s3:PutObject (uploads/*), dynamodb:PutItem, logs GetObject, Query, UpdateItem get-images dynamodb:Query, s3:GetObject (uploads/*), logs PutObject, PutItem Rekognition uses Resource: "*" because DetectModerationLabels / DetectLabels do not support resource-level permissions; only those 2 actions are granted.
AWS Well-Architected Framework mapping Pillar Measures in ImageGuard Operational Excellence Structured JSON logs; 5 EMF custom metrics (ImagesProcessed, ImagesApproved, ImagesRejected, ProcessingLatency, AlertPublishFailed); 7 alarms and the imageguard dashboard; setup.sh and step4.sh scripts for identical redeployment; moderation thresholds and blocked categories in environment variables, changeable without code changes Security See “Security design”: least privilege per Lambda, private buckets, JWT Authorizer, 5-minute presigned URLs, OAC, confused-deputy protection, no access keys or passwords in code Reliability S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS and SQS run across multiple Availability Zones; async Lambda retries 2 times then goes to the DLQ; boto3 retries 5 times on throttling; conditional writes make duplicate events harmless; bad files are marked REJECTED instead of breaking the pipeline; 35-day PITR Performance Efficiency Direct upload to S3, so the API and Lambda never receive the image; Rekognition reads from S3, so the Lambda uses no memory for the image; arm64 Lambdas, process-image 256 MB, the two API functions 128 MB; Lambda and on-demand DynamoDB scale with load; the site is cached at CloudFront edges Cost Optimization 100% serverless with nothing running 24/7; moderation before labeling; HTTP API instead of REST API; arm64; 30-day S3 Lifecycle; 14-day log retention; USD 8.37/month in Pricing Calculator (section 5.6) Sustainability Not scored by the rubric; serverless only uses resources when images arrive, and Lifecycle removes data no longer needed Key design decisions Why upload directly to S3 instead of sending the image through the API? A synchronous Lambda accepts at most 6 MB of payload (a 5 MB image in base64 exceeds it), and HTTP API bills every 512 KB as one request. A presigned URL lets the browser write exactly one file to one server-chosen key within 5 minutes: cheaper and safer.
Why create a PENDING item before issuing the URL? So process-image only processes registered uploads. A file dropped into the bucket by anyone else has no PENDING item and is ignored. The user also sees “Processing” right after the upload.
Why an async Lambda with a DLQ instead of an SQS queue between S3 and Lambda? Volumes are small, async invocations already retry twice, and the DLQ keeps failed events for reprocessing. A queue in the middle handles bursts better but adds a component the current scale does not need; it is a future step for high volumes.
Why publish to SNS after writing DynamoDB? If the email went first and the DB write failed, the Lambda retry would send duplicate emails while the image stays PENDING. This bug actually happened and was fixed (see 5.5, “Troubleshooting”).
Why do only APPROVED images get a viewing link? Violating images are never displayed again, not even to the uploader. The admin email only contains the s3Key, never an image link.
Scalability and limits Automatic scaling: Lambda adds concurrent instances when many images arrive at once; on-demand DynamoDB and S3 need no capacity planning. Limits to know: the account’s Rekognition requests-per-second quota and Lambda concurrency. Beyond them, boto3 retries, Lambda retries, and finally the event lands in the DLQ; the throttles and dlq-not-empty alarms notify the administrator. API: throttling at 10 requests/second (burst 20) protects the Lambdas and the bill from abusive callers. Next steps: an SQS queue between S3 and Lambda for bursts; AWS WAF on CloudFront; move the CLI scripts to AWS SAM/CloudFormation. Data backup The imageguard-images table has Point-in-time recovery (PITR) enabled: it can be restored to any second within the last 35 days if data is deleted or overwritten by mistake. The original images live in S3 (99.999999999% durability), so both metadata and images can be recovered.
aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name imageguard-images \ --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true # Result: ENABLED Why Region us-east-1? Low price: us-east-1 (N. Virginia) usually has the lowest prices of all Regions, including Amazon Rekognition, which is most of the cost (USD 5.91 of 8.37 per month, see section 5.6). All services available: every service used in the workshop (Rekognition Content Moderation, Cognito Managed Login, HTTP API…) is available in us-east-1. Latency is not the bottleneck: Vietnam to us-east-1 is about 200 ms, but the static site is served by CloudFront from an edge location near the user; the slowest step is AI image analysis (about 0.5–1 second), not the network. For a real deployment for Vietnamese users: move to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) to cut latency and meet personal-data rules. The Region and resource names are environment variables, so no code changes are needed. Why no VPC? There is no database or server that needs a private network. Lambda calls AWS services over HTTPS, authenticated by IAM. Putting Lambda in a VPC would add a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints (tens of USD per month) without a meaningful security gain.

Lambda, SQS and EventBridge now support payloads up to 1 MB Posted on: AWS Study Group VN (Facebook) – 06/11/2026 – https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2328196167945342/
In event-driven architecture, services exchange data through a payload (the data attached to a message or event). The old limit was 256 KB, so large data such as LLM prompts, telemetry or ML output had to be split, compressed or stored in S3.
Since early 2026, AWS has raised the limit to 1 MB for:
AWS Lambda: asynchronous invocations Amazon SQS: all messages in queues Amazon EventBridge: all events on event buses The change applies automatically to existing and new resources, with nothing to enable. If you set the SQS MaximumMessageSize attribute yourself, or wrote chunking logic around the 256 KB threshold, you may need to adjust it.
Important notes from the article:
Lambda’s 15-minute timeout and memory limits are unchanged. Parsing large JSON can use more memory and time, so load test with realistic payloads Logging full payloads to CloudWatch Logs increases cost, so log selectively or sample Every consumer must be able to handle the larger payloads The claim check pattern (store large data in S3 and pass a reference) is still useful when payloads exceed 1 MB, when multiple consumers need the data, or when audit is required For a document flow such as S3, Lambda, Textract and Bedrock, this change lets you pass more context in one message without workarounds.
Source: More room to build: serverless services now support payloads up to 1 MB – Anton Aleksandrov, Debasis Rath, AWS Compute Blog (29/01/2026) https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/more-room-to-build-serverless-services-now-support-payloads-up-to-1-mb/

Step 3 – Cognito, API Gateway, static website Step 3 can be done in the Console in the order below, or by running setup.sh in CloudShell, which creates everything with the AWS CLI (about 3 minutes).

3.1. Two API Lambdas Create 2 dedicated roles (least privilege), then 2 Python 3.12 arm64 functions, 128 MB, 10 seconds:
Lambda Inline policy permissions Environment variables imageguard-presign-upload s3:PutObject (uploads/*), dynamodb:PutItem, logs BUCKET_NAME, TABLE_NAME, URL_EXPIRES_SECONDS=300 imageguard-get-images dynamodb:Query, s3:GetObject (uploads/*), logs BUCKET_NAME, TABLE_NAME, URL_EXPIRES_SECONDS=300, MAX_ITEMS=50 presign-upload reads userId from requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims.sub, generates imageId (UUID), creates the PENDING item, then signs a presigned PUT URL. The URL is signed with the Lambda’s own permissions, so the role needs s3:PutObject.
3.2. Static website + CloudFront Bucket imageguard-web-<ACCOUNT_ID> (private, SSE-S3); upload index.html, app.js, config.js. CloudFront → Create distribution: S3 web bucket origin with OAC, Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, CachingOptimized, response headers SecurityHeadersPolicy, default root object index.html, WAF off. Bucket policy allows only cloudfront.amazonaws.com with AWS:SourceArn = the distribution ARN. Why OAC? The web bucket keeps Block all public access; only this distribution can read it. Users cannot open the S3 URL directly (tested in 5.5: 403). SecurityHeadersPolicy adds HSTS, X-Frame-Options and X-Content-Type-Options against clickjacking and MIME sniffing. WAF is not enabled yet because there is no real traffic; it is a future step.
Figure 3.2 – ImageGuard served through CloudFront
3.3. Cognito User pool imageguard-users, email sign-in, self sign-up enabled. App client SPA without a client secret: Authorization code grant, scopes openid email, callback and sign-out URL = https://<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>/. Create a domain (Managed login).
Why no client secret, and why PKCE? The web app runs entirely in the browser, so it cannot keep a secret; anyone can read the JavaScript. PKCE replaces the client secret: the browser creates a random code_verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash at sign-in and the original when exchanging the code for tokens, so an intercepted code is useless. The state parameter prevents CSRF. Tokens live in sessionStorage and disappear when the tab closes.
Figure 3.3 – Cognito Managed Login page
3.4. API Gateway HTTP API Routes POST /upload-url → presign-upload, GET /images → get-images, stage $default with auto-deploy. JWT Authorizer cognito-jwt: issuer https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<USER_POOL_ID>, audience <APP_CLIENT_ID>, attached to both routes. CORS: only origin https://<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>, headers authorization, content-type, methods GET, POST, OPTIONS. Throttling on the default route: rate 10, burst 20. Why this setup? The JWT Authorizer verifies the token signature with the User Pool’s public keys, plus issuer and audience, so forged or expired requests are rejected at API Gateway (401) without reaching Lambda or costing money (tests E3, E4 in 5.5). CORS only allows the CloudFront domain, so other websites cannot call the API from a browser. Throttling caps requests per second to protect the Lambdas and the bill.
3.5. Wire everything together CORS on the image bucket: allow PUT, GET from the CloudFront domain. Fill in config.js (Cognito domain, client ID, redirect URI, API URL), upload it again, create a CloudFront invalidation for /*. Figure 3.4 – End result: statistics, multi-image upload, and a library with status filters and label search
Figure 3.5 – Image detail dialog: labels, upload / processed time, Image ID
UI features (status filter, label search, sorting, popular labels, statistics, detail view, multi-image upload, JPEG magic-byte check, VI/EN language switch) all run in the browser on the data returned by GET /images; no new API or service is needed, so the architecture is unchanged. The chosen language is remembered in the browser; ?lang=en opens the English version directly.
Step 4 – Monitoring Run step4.sh in CloudShell, or create these in the Console:
Alarm Metric Threshold (5 minutes) imageguard-{process-image,presign-upload,get-images}-errors AWS/Lambda Errors ≥ 1 imageguard-process-image-throttles AWS/Lambda Throttles ≥ 1 imageguard-dlq-not-empty AWS/SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible ≥ 1 imageguard-alert-publish-failed ImageGuard AlertPublishFailed ≥ 1 imageguard-api-5xx AWS/ApiGateway 5xx ≥ 5 Every alarm notifies the imageguard-alerts SNS topic on both ALARM and OK. The imageguard dashboard shows APPROVED/REJECTED counts, processing time, Lambda, API Gateway, the DLQ and alarm status. Log retention is 14 days for all 3 Lambdas.
Why these alarms? Each alarm matches one failure mode: Lambda errors (errors), quota limits (throttles), events that could not be processed (dlq-not-empty), alert emails that failed to send (alert-publish-failed, a custom metric because an SNS failure does not fail the Lambda), and server-side API errors (api-5xx). The threshold is ≥ 1 because at this scale a single error deserves attention; 5xx uses ≥ 5 to avoid alerts for a single stray request. Notifications are also sent on return to OK so the administrator knows the issue cleared.
5 custom metrics (EMF): ImagesProcessed, ImagesApproved, ImagesRejected, ProcessingLatency (ms), AlertPublishFailed. The Lambda just prints one JSON line in the right format to the log and CloudWatch creates the metrics, so no cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission and no extra API calls are needed.

title: Testing and Troubleshooting
content:
Functional tests Test How Result Valid image Upload a beer image via the website APPROVED, labels Alcohol · Beer · Bottle…, shown in the gallery Violating image Upload the wooden toy gun REJECTED, blockedCategories = Violence, the admin gets an email Real user Check DynamoDB userId is the Cognito sub UUID, not an email Idempotency Overwrite the same key Log item_missing_or_already_processed, status unchanged Unknown key Upload a file with no PENDING item No new item, no email DLQ Set a wrong TABLE_NAME, invoke asynchronously After 2 retries the DLQ holds a RetriesExhausted message, approximateInvokeCount: 3 Figure: Gallery: APPROVED and REJECTED images
False positive: a wooden toy gun is detected as Violence/Weapons with ~97% confidence. Improvements: raise MIN_MODERATION_CONFIDENCE for specific categories, or add an admin review step for REJECTED images.
The DLQ test also proves least privilege: the error in the DLQ is AccessDeniedException … not authorized to perform: dynamodb:UpdateItem on resource: …table/khong-ton-tai. IAM blocks it immediately because the role can only write to imageguard-images.
Figure: DLQ message: RetriesExhausted
Success criteria check (Proposal section 3.2) Criterion Target Measured result Processing time per image ≤ 10 seconds ✅ About 0.5–1 second (ProcessingLatency metric on the dashboard) Violating images blocked ≥ 90% ❌ 2/3 (67%): both gun images blocked, one smoking image missed Valid images blocked by mistake ≤ 10% ❌ 1/8 (12.5%): a wooden toy gun was blocked (Violence/Weapons 98%); a toy water gun was approved API call without sign-in Rejected (401) ✅ {"message":"Unauthorized"} User A sees user B’s images Impossible ✅ The real user’s gallery shows only their own images although the table also holds test-user-001 items (Query by sub) Violating image detected Admin email ✅ Direct access to the S3 bucket Blocked ✅ 403 AccessDenied Both rates are measured on 12 images: the 2 initial test images plus 10 images from Wikimedia Commons, run through the real pipeline with the batch_test.sh script (26/11/2026).
Group Image Expected Result Labels / categories Normal Laptop on a desk APPROVED ✅ APPROVED Furniture, Table, Desk, Computer Normal Bicycle APPROVED ✅ APPROVED Wheel, Bicycle, Transportation Normal Pizza APPROVED ✅ APPROVED Food, Meal, Pizza Normal Cat APPROVED ✅ APPROVED Animal, Abyssinian, Cat Alcohol Beer bottle APPROVED (Alcohol allowed) ✅ APPROVED Alcohol, Beer, Bottle Tobacco Man smoking, holding a pickaxe REJECTED ❌ APPROVED Moderation only found Smoking at 27% (< 60% threshold); DetectLabels mistook the pickaxe for a Rifle Weapons Handgun REJECTED ✅ REJECTED Violence → Weapons Weapons Soldier with a rifle REJECTED ✅ REJECTED Violence → Weapons, Weapon Violence Tricky Toy water gun APPROVED ✅ APPROVED Toy, Water Gun Tricky Halloween fake-blood makeup Policy dependent REJECTED Violence → Blood & Gore (not counted in either rate) Findings and improvements:
The 60% threshold catches obvious weapons but misses smoking when the cigarette is small in the frame. Per-category thresholds (for example 25% for Drugs & Tobacco) would help, at the cost of more false positives. Gun-shaped toys are sometimes blocked, sometimes not, and fake blood counts as Blood & Gore. These cases call for an admin review step for REJECTED images instead of a hard block. 12 images is still a small sample: the results show a trend, not statistical accuracy. Security tests Test Expected Actual GET /images without a token 401 Unauthorized ✅ {"message":"Unauthorized"} Open a web-bucket file directly 403 AccessDenied ✅ only CloudFront can read it (OAC) Open an image Object URL directly 403 AccessDenied ✅ Open a presigned URL after 6 minutes Request has expired ✅ 200 before expiry, 403 after http:// Redirects to https:// ✅ 301 Moved Permanently Response headers HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy ✅ Sign-in URL contains code_challenge_method=S256 (PKCE) ✅ Figure: API without a token returns 401
Figure: Direct S3 access is denied
Figure: Direct image Object URL is denied
Figure: HTTP to HTTPS redirect and expired presigned URL
The site is served from CloudFront’s SGN (Ho Chi Minh City) edge, so Vietnamese users get fast loads even though the backend runs in us-east-1.
Error-case tests Run the error_test.sh script in CloudShell (28/11/2026). Tests E1–E3 invoke the imageguard-presign-upload Lambda directly with aws lambda invoke and bad input; E4 sends 100 parallel requests to the API; E5 uploads a text file renamed to .jpg.
# Scenario Expected Actual result E1 Request an upload URL with contentType: image/png Rejected with 400 ✅ 400 – “Chi chap nhan image/jpeg” (JPEG only) E2 Body is not JSON Rejected with 400 ✅ 400 – “Body phai la JSON” (body must be JSON) E3 No JWT (missing sub) Rejected with 401 ✅ 401 – “Unauthorized” E4 100 parallel GET /images requests without a token Blocked before reaching Lambda ✅ 100/100 returned 401 at the JWT Authorizer; Lambda was never invoked, so no cost. The 10 requests/second limit (burst 20) was not triggered in this test; not yet tested with authenticated requests E5 Text file renamed to .jpg Not stuck in PENDING, Lambda does not crash ✅ The item became REJECTED with reason INVALID_IMAGE:InvalidImageFormatException; the Lambda finished normally, so nothing went to the DLQ Figure: error_test.sh output – E1, E2 return 400; E3 and E4 return 401; E5 the invalid image is marked REJECTED
Troubleshooting 1. Inline policy: “The policy failed legacy parsing” Cause: a stray > after the Account ID in the DynamoDB ARN (…:125022369745>:table/…), so the Review page listed only 5 of 6 services. Fix: the Account ID must be 12 digits with no dashes and no < >; use Find & Replace on <ACCOUNT_ID> before pasting.
2. Alert email arrived but the item stayed PENDING Cause: at upload time the img-002 item did not match, so the conditional UpdateItem was rejected; the first version of the code published to SNS before writing the DB, so the email still went out. Lesson: that design let “unknown” uploads spam the admin. Fixed: publish to SNS only after the DB stores REJECTED; if SNS fails, log an ERROR and emit AlertPublishFailed so an alarm catches it.
The alert email was sent…
…while the item was still PENDING
3. Alarms sent no email Symptom: the alarm went to ALARM but no email arrived; the alarm history said “Failed to execute action”. Cause: the SNS topic was encrypted with the AWS managed key alias/aws/sns. CloudWatch Alarms cannot use that key (Lambda can, so REJECTED emails still arrived). Fix: disable topic encryption → history shows “Successfully executed action”. If encryption is mandatory, use a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows cloudwatch.amazonaws.com (~USD 1/month). The email only contains userId/imageId, no image or image link.
Figure: Failed to execute action
Figure: Successfully executed action after the fix
4. The Console differs from older docs New Lambda console: the role is under Custom settings → Additional settings → Custom execution role. New CloudWatch console: Log groups is now Logs → Log Management; Logs Insights is Log Analytics. A log stream shows only the last few lines: click Load more to see the image_processed line. 5. Amazon Bedrock was not available The original idea used Amazon Nova Lite on Bedrock, but every team account had a quota of 0 and the increase request was denied. The team switched to Amazon Rekognition: no quota request needed, a ready-made moderation API, and per-image pricing that is easy to estimate.

title: Cost
content:
Estimated with the AWS Pricing Calculator: view estimate.
Assumptions: us-east-1, 3,000 images/month, 1 MB per image, ~3% violating, 30,000 views; on-demand prices, before Free Tier.
Service Configuration USD/month Amazon Rekognition 3,000 DetectModerationLabels + 2,910 DetectLabels 5.91 AWS Lambda 3 arm64 functions, 36,000 invocations, 500 ms, 256 MB 0.07 Amazon API Gateway (HTTP) 33,000 requests 0.03 Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) 6,000 writes, 30,000 reads, 0.01 GB 0.01 Amazon S3 3 GB, 3,000 PUT, 30,000 GET 0.10 Amazon CloudWatch 5 EMF metrics + 7 alarms + 0.1 GB logs, 1 dashboard 2.25 CloudFront, Cognito, SNS, SQS Within the free tier 0.00 Total 8.37 (≈ USD 100/year) Actual cost of running the workshop: fewer than 300 images → about USD 0.30–0.60 for Rekognition; everything else is within the free tier.
Cost at higher volumes (linear estimate) Images/month Rekognition Other services Estimated total 3,000 5.91 2.46 ≈ USD 8.4 30,000 59.10 ≈ 4 ≈ USD 63 300,000 591.00 ≈ 25 ≈ USD 616 Rekognition is 70% of the cost at 3,000 images and over 90% at high volumes; CloudWatch is mostly fixed (alarms, dashboard). The most important optimization is therefore fewer Rekognition calls: moderation before labeling (done), and optionally turning off DetectLabels where labels are not needed. Rekognition pricing drops in tiers beyond 1 million images/month.
Cost optimization 100% serverless: no EC2, NAT Gateway or always-on resources. Moderate first, label second: violating images skip DetectLabels. Rekognition reads images directly from S3 → short, low-memory Lambda runs. arm64 Lambda is about 20% cheaper than x86. HTTP API is about 70% cheaper than REST API. S3 lifecycle deletes images after 30 days; CloudWatch Logs retention is 14 days. CloudWatch is 27% of the total; within the free tier (10 metrics, 10 alarms, 3 dashboards) it is close to zero.

title: Clean-up
content:
After grading, delete every resource to avoid charges. Follow this order because of dependencies (e.g. CloudFront must be disabled before deletion).
Deletion cannot be undone. Download any images, logs or figures you need for the report first.
1. CloudFront (first, takes ~10 minutes) CloudFront → distribution imageguard-web → Disable → wait for Disabled → Delete. Then delete the origin access control imageguard-web-oac (Security → Origin access).
2. Everything else with CloudShell ACC=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_PAGER="" # 1. Monitoring aws cloudwatch delete-dashboards --dashboard-names imageguard aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --alarm-names $(aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix imageguard --query 'MetricAlarms[].AlarmName' --output text) # 2. API Gateway + Cognito API_ID=$(aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --query "Items[?Name=='imageguard-api'].ApiId | [0]" --output text) aws apigatewayv2 delete-api --api-id "$API_ID" POOL_ID=$(aws cognito-idp list-user-pools --max-results 60 --query "UserPools[?Name=='imageguard-users'].Id | [0]" --output text) aws cognito-idp delete-user-pool-domain --user-pool-id "$POOL_ID" --domain "imageguard-$ACC" aws cognito-idp delete-user-pool --user-pool-id "$POOL_ID" # 3. Lambda + log groups for f in process-image presign-upload get-images; do aws lambda delete-function --function-name imageguard-$f aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /aws/lambda/imageguard-$f done # 4. S3 (xoa het object roi xoa bucket / empty then delete) aws s3 rb s3://imageguard-images-$ACC --force aws s3 rb s3://imageguard-web-$ACC --force # 5. DynamoDB, SNS, SQS aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name imageguard-images aws sns delete-topic --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:$ACC:imageguard-alerts aws sqs delete-queue --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/$ACC/imageguard-process-dlq # 6. IAM roles (xoa inline policy truoc / delete inline policy first) for r in process-image presign-upload get-images; do aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name imageguard-$r-role --policy-name imageguard-$r-policy aws iam delete-role --role-name imageguard-$r-role done 3. Verify S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, Cognito, SNS, SQS, CloudWatch show no resources named imageguard. Billing → Bills: no new charges on the following days. Optional: remove the imageguard-dev-2 group and the AWSCloudShellFullAccess policy from the IAM user if no longer needed.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Sharing and Feedback Throughout my 3-month internship at Amazon Web Services Vietnam Company Limited within the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program from 14/09/2026 to 14/12/2026, I experienced an immensely valuable and inspiring learning journey. Below are my candid reflections, evaluations, and suggestions from the perspective of an Artificial Intelligence student at FPT University.
Overall Program Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The AWS Vietnam office on the 26th Floor of Bitexco Financial Tower offers a modern, highly professional, and inspiring workspace with panoramic city views. Providing real AWS accounts alongside dedicated hands-on credits completely bridges the gap between academic theory and enterprise cloud implementations. 2. Support from Mentors and Program Organizers
The mentors (Mr. Lu Hoan Thien, Mr. Nguyen Gia Hung) are dedicated, enthusiastic, and possess deep technical expertise. What I appreciated most is their inquiry-based mentoring philosophy: rather than handing out quick solutions, mentors pose guiding questions that motivate students to consult official architecture documentation (AWS Architecture Center), inspect error codes, and examine CloudWatch logs to master Root Cause Analysis. 3. Relevance to Academic Major
As an Artificial Intelligence (AI) major, my prior exposure was largely focused on model training on local setups or Google Colab environments with static datasets. Participating in FCAJ made me realize that in enterprise environments, AI models deliver real value only when integrated into a robust cloud backbone: automated ingestion via S3 Event Notifications, serverless processing with AWS Lambda, secure distributed storage in DynamoDB, and granular access control via IAM and Presigned URLs. 4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
I learned to think from the mindset of a Cloud Solutions Architect: aligning architectures with the 6 pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, forecasting operating expenses using the AWS Pricing Calculator, automating cost safeguards with AWS Budgets, and drafting professional bilingual documentation. The capstone workshop project (ImageGuard) was the most impactful hands-on experience, allowing me to take an architecture from whiteboard diagrams through IAM policy refinement, debugging, and end-to-end verification. 5. Company Culture and Team Spirit
A culture grounded in openness, mutual respect, and encouraging student proactiveness. Strong collaboration within AITeamFPT: when our initial proposal encountered service quota limitations, the team collectively evaluated alternatives and pivoted smoothly to Amazon Rekognition. Community tech events (Buildrathon Kickoff, AWS Cloud & AI Day Watch Party, Cloud Mastery 1) expanded my professional network and allowed me to exchange insights with seasoned engineers across Saigon. 6. Internship Policies and Benefits
Interns enjoy access to AWS office facilities, 12 months of AWS Skill Builder Premium, hands-on cloud credits, and complimentary invitations to premium industry events. Additional Reflections Most Satisfying Experience: Watching our team’s ImageGuard solution function seamlessly end-to-end from the web frontend: users upload images, the pipeline instantly moderates inappropriate content, indexes metadata, and dispatches real-time alerts via Amazon SNS without maintaining any physical servers.
Suggestions for Future Cohorts:
Earlier AI Lab Integration: The initial weeks focus extensively on foundational networking (VPC) and compute (EC2). Introducing small labs on invoking managed AI APIs via Lambda around weeks 3–4 would help AI students maintain immediate relevance and enthusiasm for their major. Service Quota Awareness: New accounts often have zero quota for certain advanced generative AI services (such as Bedrock) that require approval lead times. Providing early notifications or predefined fallback architectures will ensure smoother project execution. Regular Technical Office Hours: Hosting weekly 45–60 minute virtual office hours on Discord or Google Meet would help interns quickly unblock common roadblocks like IAM permission errors or CORS issues. Would I Recommend the Program to Friends?
Absolutely (100%): I have been actively recommending FCAJ to junior students at FPT University. It is an exceptional program that not only equips students with cloud and AI capabilities but also instills international-standard professional work ethics. Suggestions & Future Outlook Future Goals: Immediately following the internship, I plan to leverage the provided Skill Builder Premium subscription to prepare for and achieve the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner and AWS Certified AI Practitioner certifications to solidify my career trajectory. Acknowledgments: I express my sincere and deepest gratitude to the First Cloud AI Journey organizers, mentors at AWS Vietnam, and professors at FPT University for creating this transformative opportunity and supporting me throughout these 3 months.
